text:
I need help with an open letter from our tenants' association to our property management company. We plan to post it in the lobby and send it to the local TV station. I'm the association's secretary.

Facts:
- Our building has 9 stories, 112 apartments and one elevator.
- The elevator was out of service on 41 days this year, including one stretch of 12 days in August.
- 23 of our residents are over 75, and 6 use wheelchairs or walkers.
- The management company says a new controller part is on order and should arrive in 6 to 8 weeks. They said the same thing in June.
- The city inspected the elevator in September and gave it a passing certificate.
- 74 households signed our petition asking for a second elevator. Management says that would cost about $400,000 and can't be done in this building.

About 400 words.

Before I draft, here's the plan for the letter. One choice affects everything else, so I'd like you to make it first.

**The main decision: what do we ask for?**

Your petition asks for a second elevator. The facts you've given show the current elevator is unreliable. They don't show a second one can be built. Management has already said it would cost about $400,000 and can't be done in this building, and we have nothing that contradicts that. If the letter leads with "build a second elevator," management can answer "impossible" on TV and the story ends there.

Here is what I'd suggest instead:

- **Main ask:** Fix the elevator you have, by a firm date, and protect residents who can't use the stairs whenever it's out.
- **Second-elevator ask:** Reduce it to "show us in writing why a second elevator can't be done." This keeps the petition alive and puts the burden on management, without the letter promising something we can't back up.

If you'd rather lead with the second elevator, I'll write that version. You know your members and how far they want to push.

**How the argument would run (recommended version)**

- **Grounds:**
  - So far this year the elevator has been out on 41 of 320 days, roughly one day in eight, including 12 days in a row in August.
  - In June, management said the part would arrive in 6 to 8 weeks. That window ended in August, about three months ago, and the estimate given now is the same one.
  - 23 residents are over 75, and 6 use wheelchairs or walkers. For them, the 9th floor is unreachable without the elevator.
  - 74 of 112 households (two in three) signed the petition.
- **The link between facts and demand** (it won't be stated outright): a landlord who controls the only way some tenants can get in and out of their homes has to give real dates and backup plans, not open-ended estimates.
- **The objection we'll answer before management raises it:** "The city passed it in September." A passing certificate means the elevator is safe when it runs. It doesn't mean it runs. I won't claim any outages happened after the inspection unless you tell me they did.
- **What happens if management says no:** the same estimate again, and more stretches like August with residents stuck on their floors.

**Things I need from you**

1. The name of the association and the management company, and who signs the letter (your name and title, or "the board"?).
2. Do you want specific demands with a deadline? For example: a written delivery date for the part within 14 days, notice to residents before outages, and help for residents with limited mobility during outages. I'll only put in what you approve.
3. Did any outages happen after the September inspection? If so, that's the strongest answer to the certificate.
4. Should the letter say anything about rent reductions for days without elevator service, or leave that out?

One more thing: because this is going to a TV station, I'll keep every statement about management to what they actually said and did. That keeps the letter credible and keeps the association on safe ground.

Tell me which version you want and answer what you can above, and I'll write the roughly 400-word letter.

Go with your recommended version.

1. The building is Harbor View Apartments, 220 Grant Street, so call us the Harbor View tenants' association. The management company is Keystone Property Group, and the regional manager is Diane Weller. I'll sign it: Rosa Delgado, Secretary.
2. Yes. We want three things: a written date for the repair, a stair-climbing chair and trained staff for residents who can't walk the stairs, and a rent credit for outage days. The 14-day deadline is fine.
3. I don't know.
4. Yes, put it in. We want a rent credit for outage days.

Here's the letter, about 400 words.

<final_document>
**AN OPEN LETTER TO KEYSTONE PROPERTY GROUP**
From the Harbor View Tenants' Association
Harbor View Apartments, 220 Grant Street

November 16, 2026

Ms. Diane Weller
Regional Manager, Keystone Property Group

Dear Ms. Weller,

Harbor View Apartments has nine floors, 112 apartments and one elevator. So far this year, that elevator has been out of service on 41 days, about one day in every eight. In August it was out for 12 days in a row.

For many of our neighbors, an outage is more than an inconvenience. Twenty-three residents of this building are over 75. Six use wheelchairs or walkers. When the only elevator stops, a resident in a wheelchair on an upper floor cannot get to a doctor's appointment, to the grocery store or to the street.

In June, Keystone told us a new controller part was on order and would arrive in six to eight weeks. That window closed in August. It is now November, and we are being told the same thing again: six to eight weeks.

We know the city inspected the elevator in September and issued a passing certificate. That certificate means the elevator is safe when it runs. It does not mean the elevator will run. Forty-one days out of service shows the difference.

We ask Keystone to do three things by November 30, 2026:

1. **Give tenants a written date** by which the repair will be completed.
2. **Provide a stair-climbing chair, and staff trained to use it,** so residents who cannot walk the stairs can get in and out of the building whenever the elevator is down.
3. **Credit tenants' rent** for every day the elevator is out of service.

Seventy-four of our 112 households, two in every three, also signed a petition asking for a second elevator. Keystone has told us that would cost about $400,000 and cannot be done in this building. If that is so, we ask Keystone to explain why in writing, and to include that explanation with its reply, so tenants can see what the decision is based on.

If nothing changes, we expect more of what we have had all year: another estimate, another wait, and more stretches like August, when our oldest and least mobile neighbors were cut off in their own homes.

Our members have waited since June. They asked us to make this letter public, and we are posting it in our lobby and sharing it with local news media. We look forward to your written reply by November 30.

Sincerely,

Rosa Delgado, Secretary
On behalf of the Harbor View Tenants' Association
</invoke>
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **Dates:** The letter is dated today, so the 14-day deadline falls on November 30. If you post it on a later day, change both dates.
- **Inspection:** You didn't know whether any outages came after the September inspection, so the letter doesn't say they did. It answers the certificate point with the 41 days instead. If your records show outages after September, add a sentence. That's your strongest reply to the certificate.
- **What I left out:** I didn't name an amount for the rent credit or claim anything about specific residents' floors, because neither was in what you gave me.
- **Sending it:** Consider emailing or delivering the letter to Ms. Weller before, or at the same time as, it goes to the TV station. Then nobody can say Keystone found out from the news.
